# Abstract {.unnumbered}

Individuals interested in learning about cybercrime often begin by searching for guidance on popular social media platforms. Many of these platforms host a wide range of harmful content, including video tutorials that explain how to launch cyberattacks or use cybercrime tools. On YouTube, such tutorials are often uploaded by creators with thousands of followers and attract even larger audiences. Because many of these videos can be followed with only basic technical skills, they make cybercrime accessible to a broad audience and may serve as a pathway into cybercrime, particularly among youth. As part of a broader effort to prevent cybercrime through awareness and influence campaigns, law enforcement agencies and researchers have collaborated to counter the potential impact of these tutorials. In this study, we partnered with the Cyber Offender Prevention Squad (COPS) of the Netherlands Police to deploy a series of YouTube video advertising campaigns targeting tutorials related to two forms of entry-level cybercrime: distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks and remote access trojans (RATs). We examine the engagement generated by these campaigns among the target audience, focusing on when and where engagement occurred, who was exposed to the ads, what exposed users were searching for, and which ads performed best. The results indicate that DDoS-related ads generated higher levels of engagement than RAT-related ads, while socialization-based messages achieved greater audience retention than deterrence-based messages. Analysis of the target audience (18-24 years old) further showed that the vast majority of users who viewed and engaged with the ads were estimated to be non-parents, with males comprising most of this group. These findings provide valuable insights for law enforcement agencies considering the use of online advertising campaigns as a cybercrime prevention strategy.

# Keywords {.unnumbered}

cybercrime, cybercrime-as-a-service, crime prevention, law enforcement, online advertising campaigns, YouTube, Google, DDoS attacks, remote access trojans

# Introduction

The first steps toward cybercrime often appear innocuous. A cybercriminal career frequently begins with simple searches on the clear web and mainstream social media platforms such as YouTube [@leukfeldt2026; @martineau2024]. Searches framed as "how to" queries are common [@moneva2024]. The results often include video tutorial content that inadvertently explains the fundamentals of cybercrime offending, typically under the guise of education or research [@kool2026]. In doing so, these resources can direct users toward subsequent steps in the cybercrime pathway. A few steps further, individuals may encounter fully functional cybercrime tools and services.

Cybercrime services are not offered exclusively through the dark web. Users have long relied on widely accessible clear web platforms to exchange information and trade cybercrime-related tools and services, including Google, YouTube, and various hacker forums [@kool2026; @leukfeldt2026; @martineau2024; @martineau2024]. In recent years, however, the range of available platforms and materials has expanded considerably, now encompassing other mainstream platforms such as Instagram, Telegram, Snapchat, and Discord [@roks2020; @garkava2024; @bekkers2023; @loggen2026]. Due to the algorithmic nature of content distribution on these platforms, users may inadvertently encounter cybercrime-related content, even when they are not actively searching for it. The large-scale data processing capabilities employed by these platforms can reveal patterns through the matching of related searches and interests, linking otherwise innocuous queries to potentially harmful content. This includes cybercrime tutorials that, often presented as educational material or technical guidance, provide step-by-step instructions for committing a variety of cybercrimes. Examples include launching distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks through booters---online services that offer DDoS-for-hire capabilities [@cardosodesantanna2017]---and gaining unauthorized remote access to devices using remote access trojans (RATs), a type of malware that grants attackers extensive control over compromised systems [@farinholt2019]. The commodification of cybercrime within the clear web lowers barriers to entry by making cybercriminal tools, knowledge, and services accessible to a broad audience [@hyslip2020] . Consequently, individuals with limited technical expertise may become involved in cybercriminal activities, contributing to the emergence of new offenders [@akyazi2021; @europol2023; @europol2024; @manky2013].

In response to this trend, law enforcement agencies have begun exploring novel policing strategies aimed at disrupting individuals’ early involvement in cybercrime. Among these, influence policing approaches leverage the algorithmic features of digital technologies to deliver targeted messages to individuals considered at risk of engaging in cybercriminal activities [@collier2021]. One of the most widely used mechanisms for delivering such interventions is online advertising campaigns deployed through search engines [@collier2022]. These campaigns are configured to trigger ads when users search for terms associated with cybercrime, thereby displaying intervention messages within search results. Several European law enforcement agencies, including the United Kingdom’s National Crime Agency (UK NCA) and the Netherlands Police, have pioneered this approach, deploying targeted online advertising campaigns against cybercrime since the late 2010s [@collier2019; @moneva2022]. The ads typically communicate deterrent messages, such as “DDoS is illegal”, or socializing ones, such as “DDoS ruins it for everyone”. These messages may influence behavior through different mechanisms, including increasing the perceived risk of detection and punishment or removing users’ excuses for antisocial behavior [@moneva2023]. In doing so, they seek to discourage cybercrime involvement.

Interviews with cybercrime offenders have shown that many are largely self-taught, relying on search engines to find cybercrime tutorials and learning resources [@nationalcybercrimeunit2017; @leukfeldt2026; @martineau2024]. Consequently, early influence policing campaigns focused primarily on search engines [@collier2019]. However, users also frequently rely on other online platforms to access such content, particularly YouTube [@leukfeldt2026; see also @farinholt2019; @kool2026]. There, content creators regularly publish step-by-step videos explaining how cyberattacks work. While these videos are often framed as educational resources intended to improve cybersecurity knowledge, they may simultaneously disseminate knowledge and techniques that can be misused for cybercriminal purposes [@kool2026]. Creators often have large audiences, attracting thousands of subscribers and substantial view counts. Their content is typically designed for viewers with limited technical expertise, making complex cybercrime-related skills more accessible to a broad audience. For content consumers, such videos may therefore serve as a pathway into cybercrime. Given their potential role in facilitating cybercrime initiation, these tutorials represent a relevant target for influence policing interventions.

In this study, we examine one such intervention implemented by the Netherlands Police involving a series of short video ads designed to appear alongside potential cybercrime tutorials on YouTube. The campaign targeted content related to DDoS attacks and RATs, with the aim of nudging viewers away from cybercrime involvement and discouraging engagement in cybercriminal activities. The police focused on DDoS attacks and remote access trojans (RATs) because they may serve as gateway offences [see @moneva2023] and pose significant cybersecurity risks [@europol2024]. Individuals entering cybercrime often begin with these relatively accessible activities and often rely on online video tutorials to acquire the necessary knowledge, making YouTube a particularly relevant platform for early intervention [@leukfeldt2026].

By examining the results of the first video ad campaign implemented by the Netherlands Police against cybercrime tutorials, this study contributes to the growing body of research on the application of influence policing strategies to prevent cybercrime [e.g. @collier2019; @moneva2023]. Importantly, the study does not evaluate the campaign's impact on cybercrime outcomes (i.e., whether it reduces cybercrime offending). Instead, it describes the intervention and examines the user engagement it generated. The findings can inform law enforcement agencies considering the use of such easily implemented and scalable interventions, thereby supporting evidence-based policing and the efficient allocation of resources [@moneva2022].

# Behavioral approaches to cutting initial crime involvement

One way to proactively prevent involvement in crime is by promoting behavioral change. By influencing the factors that shape individual decision-making, it may be possible to steer individuals away from offending [@thereas1986; @situatio1997]. From a classical economic perspective, individuals are assumed to weigh the costs and benefits of their actions and engage in crime when the perceived benefits outweigh the perceived costs [@becker1968]. Currently, both criminological and behavioral economic perspectives recognize that decision-making is bound rather than perfectly rational [@thereas1986; @kahneman2011]. Individuals are subject to cognitive biases, limited self-control, emotional influences, and constraints in their ability to assess future risks and consequences. Both the evaluative and cognitive processes underlying decision-making can be leveraged to influence behavior. For example, shaping aspects of the immediate environment may affect the choices individuals make, whether these influences are consciously perceived or not [@pogarsky2018; @thaler2009; @clarke2017].

In criminology, two prominent approaches to behavioral change and crime reduction are situational crime prevention (SCP) and nudging [@clarke1980; @pogarsky2019]. Situational crime prevention seeks to reduce crime opportunities by modifying situational conditions that shape offending decisions [@clarke2017]. Drawing on rational choice perspectives, SCP interventions increase the effort and risks associated with offending while reducing its rewards, provocations, and perceived justifications, thereby making crime opportunities less attractive [@cornish2003].

Nudging similarly aims to influence behavior by shaping features of the decision-making environment [@pogarsky2018]. Defined as “any aspect of the choice architecture that alters people’s behavior in a predictable way without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives” [@thaler2009, p. 6], nudges can affect both automatic, intuitive processes and more reflective, deliberative forms of decision-making. By influencing how individuals perceive and evaluate risks, rewards, and other relevant information, nudges can steer behavior while preserving freedom of choice [@pogarsky2018; @pogarsky2019].

SCP and nudging are closely related but differ in two important respects. First, SCP interventions are inherently crime-focused and are designed to influence decisions at or near the point of offending, disrupting the offender’s crime script. Nudges, in contrast, are not necessarily crime-related and can be applied across a wide range of behavioral domains. However, when deployed to prevent offending, nudges may function as a form of SCP by altering situational factors relevant to criminal decision-making [@roach2017; @moneva2023]. Second, whereas SCP often seeks to modify behavior through substantial changes to the effort, risks, and rewards associated with offending, nudges rely on more subtle changes to choice architecture. Rather than constraining options or imposing significant costs, they seek to guide behavior while preserving individuals’ autonomy to choose [@pogarsky2018; @thaler2009].

# Law enforcement interventions to change cybercrime behavior

SCP and nudging have been widely applied to conventional forms of crime and antisocial behavior, and have generally been found either effective in reducing offending or, at least, not producing adverse outcomes [@situatio1997; @guerette2009; @maier2022]. The growing importance of cybercrime services in facilitating entry into cybercrime has similarly attracted the attention of law enforcement agencies, encouraging the development of innovative prevention strategies. One example was implemented by the UK NCA, which used Google Ads to display warning messages to users searching for DDoS-for-hire services through booter-related terms [@collier2019]. These ads emphasized the illegality of DDoS attacks and directed users to a dedicated website providing information on the legal consequences of offending, the harms experienced by victims, and legitimate pathways for developing cybersecurity skills [@moneva2022].

Empirical research evaluating online ad campaigns against cybercrime remains limited. The few studies conducted to date have examined the engagement generated by these interventions [@moneva2022], their ability to reach the intended audience [@moneva2024], and, most importantly, their effectiveness in reducing DDoS attacks [@collier2019; @moneva2023]. Initial findings suggested that such campaigns may exert a temporary deterrent effect. For example, although DDoS activity increased in several countries, attack volumes in the United Kingdom remained relatively stable during the implementation of an NCA advertising campaign [@collier2019]. However, subsequent research checked the robustness of these findings. Using the same data source but a different research design, a quasi-experimental evaluation of seven campaigns implemented across 12 European countries revealed mixed results [@moneva2023]: most campaigns showed no significant effects, one was associated with a reduction in DDoS attacks, and another with an increase. Overall, the evidence neither provided support for the effectiveness of online advertising campaigns in reducing DDoS offending, nor conclusively ruled out the possibility of an effect.

Despite mixed evidence regarding their effectiveness, law enforcement agencies continue to view online advertising campaigns as a promising tool for delivering large-scale, cost-effective interventions to hard-to-reach populations. To extend their reach, recent campaigns have expanded from text-based search ads to video-based platforms, leveraging the persuasive power of audiovisual content to communicate preventive messages.

# The current study

In this study, we examine the extent to which the video advertising campaigns against cybercrime deployed by the Cyber Offender Prevention Squad (COPS) of the Netherlands Police in 2023--2024 functioned as an effective means of communicating cybercrime prevention messages. To do so, we analyze YouTube users’ engagement with a series of tailored ads targeting two forms of entry-level cybercrime: DDoS attacks and RATs. The central research question is:

> How does user engagement vary for different video ads against cybercrime tutorials on YouTube?

To answer this question, we break it down into five sub-questions that examine the campaign’s performance and user interactions in greater detail. Specifically, we investigate:

> When did the campaign generate engagement? We analyse temporal patterns in user engagement metrics over the course of the campaign.

> When and where were the ads displayed? We provide an overview of the times and regions in which users were exposed to the campaign.

> Who was exposed to the ads? We examine engagement metrics across demographic segments.

> What were users searching for when they were exposed to the ads? We analyse interaction metrics in relation to the keywords associated with ad delivery.

> Which ads generated the highest and lowest levels of engagement? We compare engagement metrics across the four ads, with a particular focus on impressions and viewing behaviour.

# Methods

To address the research question, we collaborated with the Cyber Offender Prevention Squad (COPS) of the Netherlands Police to design and deploy a quasi-experimental video advertising campaign on YouTube. The campaign targeted Dutch- and English-speaking users in the Netherlands. The intention was to target specific cybercrime-related tutorials on YouTube. However, because direct targeting of individual videos was not possible, we had to rely on a second-best, less precise strategy that targeted users based on their searches and inferred interests. Ad delivery was linked to users’ prior searches for keywords related to DDoS attacks or RATs on YouTube or Google Search. Users who had searched for such terms could subsequently encounter one of the campaign ads while watching content on YouTube. However, due to the opaque nature of YouTube's ad delivery algorithms, it is unclear how ads were prioritized among eligible users or when they were displayed. This means that ads may have been viewed either while users were consuming content directly related to their search query or at a later, algorithmically determined point in time (potentially a few days after the original search).

## A YouTube Ads video campaign

The advertising campaign consisted of two ad groups: one targeting DDoS attacks and the other targeting the use of RATs. The campaign employed a $2×2$ factorial design, resulting in four distinct ads delivered as skippable in-stream videos (@fig-videos). The first factor was the type of cybercrime featured in the ad---DDoS attacks or unauthorized remote access---while the second was the preventive mechanism employed: deterrence or socialization. The ads were informed by police expertise and co-developed with an external marketing agency that provided expertise in audiovisual communication. The deterrent ad featured a uniformed police officer in an interrogation room speaking directly to the viewer. The video was identical in both the DDoS and RAT campaigns, with the only difference being the offence type referenced by the officer. In contrast, the socialization ads depicted the potential consequences of engaging in each form of cybercrime. The DDoS ad illustrated how a cyberattack disrupted emergency services, resulting in delays in ambulance response to a traffic accident. The RAT ad portrayed the consequences of the non-consensual dissemination of intimate images, showing a young person contacting a suicide helpline. All ads concluded with the same nudging message, emphasizing a choice between criminal and legitimate pathways in cybersecurity: *“You choose. Will you become a cybercriminal or a cyberprofessional?”* (Dutch: *“Jij kiest. Word je cybercrimineel of cyberprofessional?”*). The full video ads are available through the [Open Science Framework (OSF)](https://osf.io/dyn6g/files/osfstorage). Participants were unaware of the experimental condition to which they had been exposed.

## Campaign deployment

@fig-timeline provides a timeline of the entire campaign deployment. To determine the most suitable campaign design [see @google2024e], we first launched a non-skippable video advertising campaign aimed at maximizing brand awareness and reach. This testing phase ran for 115 days, from 9 August to 31 December 2023, and allowed us to test different campaign parameters and assess their performance. Insights gained during this phase indicated that a skippable format offered a more efficient approach to reaching the target audience. When delivered as skippable in-stream video ads, ads can appear before, during, or after YouTube videos and content hosted on websites and applications within Google's video partner network. After five seconds, viewers are given the option to skip the ad and continue watching their selected content. We subsequently conducted a pilot study using the skippable format, which ran for 96 days, from 29 October 2023 to 31 January 2024. After confirming that the campaign was effectively reaching the intended audience, we launched the final campaign on 1 February 2024. The campaign was deployed through Google Ads platform using the *efficient reach* setting, which is designed to maximize the number of unique users reached while minimizing costs [@google2024d], and ran continuously until 8 April 2024, for a total of 68 days.

## Targeting

The target population consisted of users actively searching for (illegal) tools associated with DDoS attacks and RATs. Given prior evidence that individuals involved in DDoS attacks and RAT-related offending tend to be relatively young [@loggen2024], the campaign targeted users in the youngest adult age category (18–24 years). Google derives demographic information about users through several sources, including self-reported profile data, information obtained from third-party platforms, and behavioral inferences based on users’ activity across Google’s advertising network [see @google2024]. Age is categorized into the groups 18--24, 25--34, 35--44, 45--54, 55--64, 65+, and unknown, while gender is classified as female, male, or unknown. Google also estimates users’ parental status, classifying them as parent, not a parent, or unknown. The Unknown category includes users whose demographic characteristics cannot be determined, as well as minors, whose information is not disclosed for privacy reasons.

To precisely target this population segment, we combined a content-targeting method (keywords) with an audience-targeting method (custom segments) [@google2026]. First, 114 keywords were applied to the campaign's content settings to target relevant YouTube videos, channels, and metadata directly related to DDoS attacks or RATs.[^1] Second, these same keywords were used to create a custom segment based on user interests, reaching users who had actively entered these terms into Google Search or YouTube. Consequently, the available audience pool was substantially narrowed: ads were delivered only to users who both had search histories related to the campaign and were actively consuming relevant content. 

[^1]: Unlike traditional search campaigns, keywords do not function as strict matching constraints (e.g. phrase match or exact match). Instead, all keywords operate as broad matches by default, allowing ads to appear alongside content related to the specified keywords.

We did not specify a target sample size in advance, as the campaign was constrained by a fixed advertising budget. Instead, the goal was to maximize reach within the available resources.

## Interaction metrics

To examine the extent to which users watched and interacted with the ads, and campaign performance, we draw on several metrics provided by YouTube [see @google2024b]:

**Impressions**: The number of times the video ad began playing. When available, we used *viewable impressions*, defined as instances in which at least 50% of the ad’s pixels were visible on the user’s screen for a minimum of two consecutive seconds while the video was playing. Ads may be served but not viewed due to immediate user abandonment, background playback, or network-related issues.

**Views**: The number of times a user watched at least 30 seconds of the ad (or the full duration if the video was shorter than 30 seconds), or clicked on the ad before reaching that threshold. *View rates* represent the ratio of views to impressions. *Engaged views* represent the number of times a user watched a skippable in-stream ad for at least 10 consecutive seconds (or its full duration if shorter) without clicking or skipping the ad. *Video played to x%* indicates the proportion of viewers who watched 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100% of the ad, calculated relative to all users who initiated video playback. *Watch time* measures the amount of time users spent watching the video ad, measured in seconds. This metric can also be expressed as the *average watch time per impression*.

**Clicks**: The number of times users clicked on a companion banner or call-to-action link directing them from YouTube to an external landing page. In Google Ads reporting, a click is also recorded as a view and an engagement. *Click-through rates (CTR)* represent the ratio of clicks to impressions.

**Cost**: The total expenditure on the campaign, reported in euros (€). This metric can also be presented as *cost-per-thousand impressions (CPM)*. We adopted a target CPM bidding strategy of €65. Because the campaign never reached its daily budget limit, ad delivery remained unrestricted, enabling maximum exposure among the target audience throughout the study period.

**Engagements**: The number of interactions users performed with ad features while remaining within the YouTube environment, such as clicking on information cards or other small interactive elements. These features are embedded within videos and enable users to navigate to related videos, playlists, channels, or external web pages.

# Results

## Campaign metrics over time

@fig-campaign-time presents the performance of the final campaign over time, measured in terms of impressions, views, clicks, and view rates. During the study period, the ads generated 49,196 viewable impressions, 16,204 engagements, 9,789 views, and 177 clicks.

When examining daily interaction metrics in Panel a), impressions increased sharply at the start of the campaign before reaching a plateau. Following this initial surge, impression volumes declined and remained relatively stable for approximately one month. It was during this plateau that the view rate remained at its highest levels, staying between 20% and 25% for an extended period. A second increase subsequently occurred, followed by a similar plateau to the first one, suggesting a possible seasonal pattern, although the underlying cycle remains unclear.[^2] Trends in views closely mirrored those observed for impressions. Clicks also increased during the major peaks in impressions, particularly in early February and late March. However, compared with impressions and views, click volumes appeared less sensitive to fluctuations in campaign reach.

[^2]: One possible explanation for these spikes is that high-profile DDoS incidents increased the volume of related searches, resulting in greater ad delivery [@collier2019; @moneva2022]. However, we found no evidence linking the observed peaks to specific incidents in the Netherlands. Alternatively, the fluctuations may reflect changes in Google’s ad delivery algorithms, although this could not be verified due to the platform’s limited transparency.

Panel b) presents campaign performance by time of day. Visual inspection indicates that the number of impressions began to increase around 06:00, continued rising throughout the morning, and peaked at approximately 3,000 impressions around 14:00. Impression volumes then remained relatively stable until 22:00, after which they declined steadily, reaching roughly 500 impressions by 03:00. A different pattern emerged for the view rate. Although the absolute numbers of impressions and views decreased during the night, the proportion of users who watched the ads increased substantially. The view rate began rising at approximately 23:00, continued to increase throughout the night, and peaked at around 27.5% at 03:00. Thereafter, it declined and stabilized between 17.5% and 22.5% during daytime hours. This suggests that users exposed to the ads during nighttime hours were more likely to watch them than users reached during the day, despite lower overall levels of ad delivery.

## Geographical coverage

```{r}
#| label: prepare-map

# Load Dutch provincial boundary polygons from the PDOK/CBS geospatial service
poly_nl_provinces <- st_read(
  dsn = "WFS:https://service.pdok.nl/cbs/gebiedsindelingen/2021/wfs/v1_0",
  layer = "gebiedsindelingen:provincie_gegeneraliseerd",
  quiet = TRUE
) |> 
  # Recode province names to prepare for merging
  mutate(province = recode_values(
    x = statnaam,
    "Fryslân" ~ "Friesland",
    "Noord-Holland" ~ "North Holland",
    "Zuid-Holland" ~ "South Holland",
    "Noord-Brabant" ~ "North Brabant",
    default = statnaam
  ))

df_location_summary <- df_location_ |> 
  group_by(location) |> 
  summarise(
    sum_impr = sum(impr),
    sum_views = sum(views),
    sum_cost = sum(cost),
    sum_clicks = sum(clicks)
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  mutate(
    view_rate_aggr = round((sum_views / sum_impr) * 100, 1),
    avg_cpm_aggr = round(sum_cost / (sum_impr / 1000), 2),
    ctr_aggr = round((sum_clicks / sum_impr) * 100, 1),
    # Rename the key variable for the join
    province = location,
    sum_impr_p = round((sum_impr / sum(sum_impr)) * 100, 1),
    sum_views_p = round((sum_views / sum(sum_views)) * 100, 1),
    sum_cost_p = round((sum_cost / sum(sum_cost)) * 100, 1),
    sum_clicks_p = round((sum_clicks / sum(sum_clicks)) * 100, 1)
  )

df_map <- poly_nl_provinces |> 
  # Join values based on province names in the polygon file. This intentionally drops the row 'Netherlands', which is some sort of 'other' category that doesn't make sense to plot in a map, as it covers the entire territory
  left_join(
    y = df_location_summary,
    by = "province")
```

To examine how user engagement with the campaign was distributed across the Netherlands, we mapped campaign interaction metrics for each of the country's 12 provinces: Drenthe, Flevoland, Friesland, Gelderland, Groningen, Limburg, North Brabant, North Holland, Overijssel, South Holland, Utrecht, and Zeeland (@fig-base-choropleth). As expected, the most densely populated provinces, particularly South Holland and North Holland, accounted for the largest volumes of raw interactions (impressions, views, and clicks) and, consequently, the highest advertising costs. The rate-based metrics, however, tell a different story. View rates were highest in Limburg, Drenthe, and Flevoland, despite these provinces exhibiting average or below-average costs per thousand impressions (CPM). Limburg also recorded the highest CTR, alongside Friesland, although differences were small---approximately 0.2 percentage points across provinces. These geographic patterns provide insight into where the campaign was most effective and cost-efficient in generating user engagement.[^3]

[^3]: A small proportion of interactions could not be assigned to a specific province (`r df_location_summary |> filter(province == "Netherlands") |> select(sum_impr_p:sum_clicks_p) |> min()`--`r df_location_summary |> filter(province == "Netherlands") |> select(sum_impr_p:sum_clicks_p) |> max()`%. These observations were therefore aggregated at the national level and are not displayed in the provincial maps.

## Ad performance

Next, we examined the performance of the four individual video ads. View rates ranged from 13.7% to 23.6%, exceeding the average benchmarks reported by Google for skippable in-stream ads [@google2024b]. Overall, ads related to DDoS attacks generated greater engagement than those related to RATs, as reflected in higher view rates, engagement rates, and average watch time per impression (@tbl-ads). More specifically, DDoS ads generated more views and engagements than RATs ads, while within each offence category, socializing ads outperformed deterrent ads based on these measures. We used chi-square tests to assess whether views differed significantly across the four video ads. All pairwise comparisons revealed statistically significant differences at the $\alpha = .05$ level (@tbl-chisq). In contrast, CTR were largely comparable across the four ads. This suggests that although the likelihood of viewing and engaging with an ad varied considerably by message type and offence category, the ads were similarly effective in prompting users to click through to the associated webpages.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ads
#| tbl-cap: Interaction metrics by ad

df_ads_ |> 
  mutate(ad = paste(ad_name, ad_group)) |> 
  group_by(ad) |> 
  summarise(
    sum_viewable_impr = sum(viewable_impr),
    sum_views = sum(views),
    sum_clicks = sum(clicks),
    sum_engagements = sum(engagements),
    sum_watch_time = sum(watch_time)
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  mutate(
    ad_ = recode_values(
      x = ad,
      "deter ddos" ~ "DDoS attacks (deterrent)",
      "deter rat" ~ "RATs (deterrent)",
      "empathie ddos" ~ "DDoS attacks (socializing)",
      "empathie rat" ~ "RATs (socializing)"
    ),
    view_rate_ = (sum_views / sum_viewable_impr) * 100,
    engagement_rate_ = (sum_engagements / sum_viewable_impr) * 100,
    ctr_ = (sum_clicks / sum_viewable_impr) * 100,
    avg_watch_time_impr_ = (sum_watch_time / sum_viewable_impr)
  ) |> 
  select(
    ad_,
    view_rate_:avg_watch_time_impr_
  ) |> 
  arrange(desc(view_rate_)) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    ad_ = "Ad",
    view_rate_ = "View rate (%)",
    engagement_rate_ = "Engagement rate (%)",
    ctr_ = "Click-through rate (%)",
    avg_watch_time_impr_ = "Mean no. of seconds watched per impression" 
  ) |> 
  cols_width(columns = everything() ~ px(120)) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = view_rate_:avg_watch_time_impr_,
    decimals = 1
  ) 
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-chisq

df_chisq <- df_ads_ |> 
  mutate(ad = paste(ad_name, ad_group)) |> 
  group_by(ad) |> 
  summarise(
    sum_viewable_impr = sum(viewable_impr),
    sum_views = sum(views),
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  # Calculate non-views
  mutate(non_views = sum_viewable_impr - sum_views) |> 
  select(- sum_viewable_impr)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-chisq
#| tbl-cap: Pairwise comparison of ad views using Chi-squared tests of independence with Yates' continuity correction (*df* = 1)

# Function to compute pairwise Chi-Square Test of independence
compute_chisq <- function (data, ad1, ad2) {
  
  data |> 
    filter(ad %in% c(ad1, ad2)) |> 
    column_to_rownames("ad") |> 
    chisq.test() |> 
    tidy() |> 
    mutate(comparison = paste(ad1, ad2, sep = "-"))
  
}

bind_rows(
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "deter ddos", ad2 = "deter rat"),
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "deter ddos", ad2 = "empathie ddos"),
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "deter ddos", ad2 = "empathie rat"),
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "deter rat", ad2 = "empathie ddos"),
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "deter rat", ad2 = "empathie rat"),
  df_chisq |> compute_chisq(ad1 = "empathie ddos", ad2 = "empathie rat")
) |> 
  select(
    comparison,
    statistic,
    p.value,
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    comparison = recode_values(
      x = comparison,
      "deter ddos-deter rat" ~ "DDoS attacks (deterrent) vs. RATs (deterrent)",
      "deter ddos-empathie ddos" ~ "DDoS attacks (deterrent) vs. DDoS attacks (socializing)",
      "deter ddos-empathie rat" ~ "DDoS attacks (deterrent) vs. RATs (socializing)",
      "deter rat-empathie ddos" ~ "RATs (deterrent) vs. DDoS attacks (socializing)",
      "deter rat-empathie rat" ~ "RATs (deterrent) vs. RATs (socializing)",
      "empathie ddos-empathie rat" ~ "DDoS attacks (socializing)	vs. RATs (socializing)"
    ),
    sig = case_when(
      p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p.value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p.value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      .default = NA_character_
    )
  ) |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    comparison = "Comparison",
    statistic = "Statistic",
    p.value = "p-value",
    sig = "Sig."    
  ) |> 
  fmt_number(
    columns = where(is.double),
    decimals = 3
  ) |> 
  tab_footnote(
    footnote = "Note: p < .05 (*), p < .01 (**), p < .001 (***)."
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: prepare-video-played

df_ads_video_played <- df_ads_ |> 
  mutate(ad = paste(ad_name, ad_group)) |> 
  select(
    ad,
    day_of_the_week,
    video_played_to_25:video_played_to_100
  ) |> 
  group_by(ad) |> 
  summarise(
    # Add a value of 100% retention for 0% video played for visualization
    mean_video_played_to_0 = 100,
    mean_video_played_to_25 = mean(video_played_to_25),
    mean_video_played_to_50 = mean(video_played_to_50),
    mean_video_played_to_75 = mean(video_played_to_75),
    mean_video_played_to_100 = mean(video_played_to_100)
  ) 
```

To further examine viewing behavior, we analysed audience retention across the four video ads. Retention followed a similar 'slide' pattern for all videos (@fig-video-played). At the 25% playback mark (3.8 seconds), between `r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_25) |> min() |> round(1)`--`r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_25) |> max() |> round(1)`% of viewers remained. By the halfway point (7.5 seconds), retention had fallen below 50% (`r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_50) |> min() |> round(1)`--`r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_50) |> max() |> round(1)`%), likely due to the skip button becoming available after the first five seconds of playback. Thereafter, retention continued to decline at a slower rate. By the 75% playback mark (11.3 seconds), between `r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_75) |> min() |> round(1)`--`r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_75) |> max() |> round(1)`% of viewers were still watching, while `r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_100) |> min() |> round(1)`--`r df_ads_video_played |> pull(mean_video_played_to_100) |> max() |> round(1)`% watched the videos through to completion (15 seconds). Although the DDoS deterrent ad achieved the highest retention during most of the video, the DDoS socialization ad overtook it after the 75% playback mark and ultimately retained the largest proportion of viewers until completion.


## The audience

```{r}
#| label: tbl-audience
#| tbl-cap: Engagement with the ad groups by demographic characteristics

tbl_demographics_ <- df_demographics_ |> 
  filter(viewable_impr > 0) |> 
  arrange(ad_group, desc(viewable_impr)) |> 
  group_by(ad_group) |>
  mutate(
    view_rate_ = round((views / viewable_impr) * 100, 1),
    engagement_rate_ = round((engagements / viewable_impr) * 100, 1),
    viewable_impr_p = round((viewable_impr / sum(viewable_impr)) * 100, 1),
    engagements_p = round((engagements / sum(engagements)) * 100, 1),
    views_p = round((views / sum(views)) * 100, 1)
  ) |> 
  select(
    ad_group,
    gender,
    parental_status,
    viewable_impr,
    viewable_impr_p,
    engagements,
    engagements_p,
    views,
    views_p,
    view_rate_,
    engagement_rate_
  )

# Create helper datasets for inline references to specific values
tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents <- tbl_demographics_ |> 
  filter(parental_status == "Not a parent") |> 
  group_by(ad_group) |> 
  summarise(
    sum_viewable_impr_p = sum(viewable_impr_p),
    sum_engagements_p = sum(engagements_p),
    sum_views_p = sum(views_p)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents_male <- tbl_demographics_ |> 
  filter(parental_status == "Not a parent") |> 
  group_by(ad_group, gender) |> 
  summarise(
    sum_viewable_impr_p = sum(viewable_impr_p),
    sum_engagements_p = sum(engagements_p),
    sum_views_p = sum(views_p),
    .groups = "drop_last"
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  filter(gender == "Male")

tbl_demographics_ |> 
  gt() |> 
  cols_label(
    ad_group = "Ad group",
    gender = "Gender",
    parental_status = "Parental status",
    viewable_impr = "n",
    viewable_impr_p = "%",
    views = "n",
    views_p = "%",
    view_rate_ = "View rate (%)",
    engagements = "n",
    engagements_p = "%",
    engagement_rate_ = "Engagement rate (%)"
  ) |> 
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Viewable impressions",
    columns = starts_with(match = "viewable")
  ) |> 
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Views",
    columns = starts_with(match = "views")
  ) |> 
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Engagements",
    columns = starts_with(match = "engagements")
  ) |> 
  tab_row_group(
    label = "RATs ads",
    rows = 8:14
  ) |> 
  tab_row_group(
    label = "DDoS attacks ads",
    rows = 1:7,
  ) |> 
  cols_width(viewable_impr:engagement_rate_ ~ px(50)) |> 
  cols_align(
    columns = viewable_impr:engagement_rate_,
    align = "right"
  ) |> 
  tab_options(table.font.size = pct(50))
```

@tbl-audience summarizes the demographic characteristics of users exposed to the ads. The vast majority of users were classified as non-parents across all interaction metrics, including viewable impressions, engagements, and views (between `r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents |> filter(ad_group == "ddos") |> select(-ad_group) |> min()`--`r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents |> filter(ad_group == "ddos") |> select(-ad_group) |> max()`% for the DDoS attacks videos, and `r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents |> filter(ad_group == "rat") |> select(-ad_group) |> min()`--`r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents |> filter(ad_group == "rat") |> select(-ad_group) |> max()`% for the RATs videos). Among these users, males constituted a substantial majority (between `r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents_male |> filter(ad_group == "ddos") |> select(-c(ad_group, gender)) |> min()`--`r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents_male |> filter(ad_group == "ddos") |> select(-c(ad_group, gender)) |> max()`%, and `r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents_male |> filter(ad_group == "rat") |> select(-c(ad_group, gender)) |> min()`--`r tbl_demographics_summary_non_parents_male |> filter(ad_group == "rat") |> select(-c(ad_group, gender)) |> max()`%, respectively). A smaller but notable proportion of users exposed to the DDoS ads were identified as parents (`r tbl_demographics_ |> filter(ad_group == "ddos", parental_status == "Parent") |> summarize(sum(viewable_impr_p)) |> pull()`% of the users exposed to the videos). Interestingly, this subgroup exhibited the highest engagement rate among all demographic categories. The remaining demographic groups accounted for only a small share of the audience, often generating fewer than 100 interactions. Given these limited numbers, we consider the corresponding results exploratory and refrain from interpreting them in detail. This audience profile aligns with existing research indicating that cyber-dependent offenders are predominantly young males, while there is little evidence suggesting that such offenders are typically parents [see @loggen2024 for a systematic review].

## Keywords

This section examines the six most frequently searched keywords associated with users who were exposed to the ads, grouped by ad group and the device on which the ad was displayed (@fig-keywords). In both categories, a single keyword dominated the searches. For the DDoS ads, the most common keyword was "download booter". The remaining top DDoS-related keywords were likewise associated with either learning how to conduct DDoS attacks or identifying services that facilitate them. For the RATs ads, the dominant keyword was "Venom software", referring to an information-stealing malware service designed to extract sensitive data, such as passwords, browser credentials, cookies, and cryptocurrency wallet information, from compromised systems. Notably, five of the six most frequently searched keywords in this category referred directly to malware or RAT variants, including NonoCore, Revcode WebMonitor, and FUD (Fully UnDetectable). The term "malicious APK" similarly refers to malware, although it encompasses a broader category of malicious Android application packages. Finally, CAV (Counter Antivirus) refers to tools used to test whether malware can evade antivirus detection, technologies commonly employed by malware developers and distributors. In line with expectations based on the predefined keywords, the keyword distributions suggest that the campaign primarily reached users searching for information about offensive cybercrime tools and services rather than general cybersecurity content, indicating that the ads were delivered to a population broadly aligned with the intended target audience.

Ads for both DDoS attacks and RATs were delivered across four device types, with mobile phones accounting for most viewable impressions, followed by computers. Because Google accounts are typically used across multiple devices, it is not possible to determine which device users originally conducted the searches that triggered ad delivery. For example, a user may have searched for a term such as "download booter" on a computer but subsequently encountered the ad while watching YouTube on a mobile phone using the same Google account. A notable observation is that many of the searches associated with both the DDoS and RAT campaigns were explicitly related to downloading booters or malware tools. Although such downloads can also be performed on mobile devices, these activities are generally more practical and convenient on computers. Consequently, the predominance of mobile ad delivery should not be interpreted as evidence that users primarily searched for or intended to use these tools on mobile devices. Rather, it likely reflects cross-device behavior within users’ Google accounts and broader patterns of YouTube consumption.

# Discussion

In this study, we analyzed the performance of a video advertising campaign designed to reach and engage individuals at risk of becoming involved in cybercrime. Consistent with the cybercrime prevention strategy of the Netherlands Police, the campaign aimed to inform users at an early stage of cybercrime involvement and steer them away from a pathway into cybercrime. Four short video ads were conceived as nudges targeting users searching for content related to DDoS attacks and RATs. By appearing alongside cybercrime tutorials on YouTube, or after users had searched for cybercrime-related content, the ads sought to redirect users towards prosocial behavior alternatives and discourage engagement in cybercriminal activities. Our quasi-experimental factorial design allowed us to compare two preventive approaches, deterrence and socialization, across the two forms of cybercrime. This design helped us determine how both the offence type and the preventive message influenced user engagement with the ads.

The campaign generated substantial engagement relative to cross-industry averages reported by Google [@google2024b]. In particular, the DDoS ads substantially outperformed the upper benchmark of 15%, achieving view rates that were 6 – 9 percentage points higher---approximately 50% above the industry average. Across both offence types, the socializing ads consistently and slightly outperformed the deterrent ones, aligning with previous findings that socialization messages tend to generate greater engagement than deterrent ones [@moneva2022]. With view rates ranging from 14% to 24%, approximately one in five users watched or engaged with the ads, indicating that the campaign was successful in attracting attention from its target audience.

Temporal and geographical patterns of engagement with the ads were not uniform. As observed in previous anti-DDoS text-based advertising campaigns [@moneva2022], view rates peaked during nighttime hours, a finding consistent with the possibility that individuals interested in cybercrime-related content are more active online at these times. Geographically, the highest engagement rates were observed in provinces with low to moderate population density, rather than in the country's most densely populated areas. This pattern may reflect differences in audience composition, advertising competition, or regional media consumption habits. However, given the limited transparency of Google's ad-delivery mechanisms, it is not possible to determine whether these differences resulted from user behavior, platform optimization processes, or a combination of both.

When examining the audience reached by the campaign, we observed a well-established pattern in cybercrime research: males engaged with the content at disproportionately higher rates than females [see @loggen2024]. Beyond corroborating previous research, the findings extend the literature on cybercrime interest by exploring the relationship between parenthood and engagement with cybercrime prevention ads. According to Google’s sociodemographic estimates, most interactions originated from users classified as non-parents. Interestingly, however, a smaller group of users identified as parents also engaged with the ads and exhibited the highest engagement rates of all demographic categories. This finding is broadly consistent with life-course and routine activity perspectives, which suggest that family roles and other forms of informal social control may structure daily routines and reduce engagement in unstructured activities [@buil-gil2026; @sampson1997]. Individuals with fewer family obligations, such as non-parents, may have more spare time and, consequently, greater exposure to cybercrime-related content and opportunities. Although the number of parents reached by the campaign was relatively small, those who encounter such content may be particularly motivated to seek further information. One possible explanation is that parents engage with cybercrime-related content out of concern for their children online activities and potential exposure to cybercrime risks. Another possibility is that children use their parents' devices to search for cybercrime-related content and interact with the video ads on them.

Consistent with the intended keyword targeting strategy, the keyword analysis suggests that the campaign successfully reached users actively searching for potentially illicit content. For the DDoS campaign, the most common searches were related to DDoS tools and attack methods used to overwhelm websites and internet services with malicious traffic. Similarly, users exposed to the RAT ads frequently searched for malware tools and evasion techniques associated with unauthorized remote access, smartphone compromise, and the circumvention of antivirus detection. These findings indicate that the ads were broadly delivered to the intended audience of individuals expressing interest in offensive cyber capabilities.

Overall, both the audience and keyword analyses suggest that the campaign's targeting strategy was well aligned with its intended purpose.These findings indicate that collaboration between police prevention specialists, crime researchers, and marketing professionals can be an effective approach to designing and implementing interventions that not only reach individuals interested in cybercrime-related content but also successfully engage them. Whether these promising engagement outcomes translate into meaningful reductions in cybercrime involvement, however, remains an open question. While the campaign demonstrated its ability to reach and attract the attention of the target audience, its impact on subsequent behaviour cannot be determined from the present study. Assessing whether such interventions ultimately reduce offending or discourage progression into cybercrime therefore remains an important avenue for future research.

Given that pathways into cybercrime often begin on mainstream online platforms, prevention efforts such as advertising campaigns should not be viewed solely as the responsibility of law enforcement agencies. Platform providers are uniquely positioned to contribute to prevention. They have extensive data about both user behavior and the content hosted on their platforms, which could be used to identify and remove harmful content, or restrict its access to specific audiences. At the same time, search, recommendation, and content moderation systems could be leveraged to deliver preventive interventions and promote prosocial alternatives to at-risk users. By adopting a largely passive role in this regard, mainstream platforms such as YouTube and Google facilitate the early stages of cybercrime involvement.

# Limitations

To conclude, several limitations should be taken into account when interpreting the findings of this study.

First, we do not know the extent to which ad-blocking technologies reduced the reach of the video advertising campaign. Throughout most of 2024, conventional ad blockers were still capable of blocking skippable YouTube ads, although YouTube’s increasingly aggressive anti-ad-blocking measures created an ongoing technological 'cat and mouse' game between the platform and ad-blocking software. Consequently, some members of the target audience may never have been exposed to the campaign, potentially affecting its overall reach.

Second, one of the primary objectives of the intervention was to reach individuals in the early stages of a potential cybercriminal trajectory. However, accurately identifying this population is challenging because legal and platform-level restrictions substantially limit the targeting of minors. Google, for instance, prohibits advertisers from targeting users under the age of 18 based on personal interests or behavioral data [@google2024f]. Although minors could still encounter the ads through contextual keyword matching, their demographic information is not disclosed and is instead aggregated into Google's Unknown category. As a result, we cannot determine the extent to which the campaign reached younger audiences, despite this group being particularly relevant from a prevention perspective.

Third, the campaign relied on a third-party platform---Google Ads---for ad delivery. The mechanisms governing how ads were distributed, including the criteria used to determine which ads were shown and when, are only partially transparent. This limited visibility constrains our ability to assess the extent to which observed outcomes were driven by campaign characteristics or by Google's proprietary ad-delivery systems. For example, we were unable to explain the two pronounced spikes in viewable impressions observed during the campaign. Beyond complicating the interpretation of the findings, this lack of transparency also poses challenges for the reproducibility and replicability of research conducted on commercial advertising platforms.

Fourth, and related to the previous point, future evaluations of the campaign's effects on offending should consider that the ads may have been shown several days after a user conducted a relevant search. This delay could have reduced the intervention's salience at the moment of decision-making, limiting its potential to change behavior.

# Data availability statement

The data and code necessary to reproduce the analyses presented in this paper, except for the keyword analyses, are publicly available at [Open Science Framework (OSF)](https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/DYN6G).

The keyword list used for audience targeting is not publicly available because its disclosure could facilitate access to cybercrime-related services. Instead, the keyword list is available upon request to: 1) researchers seeking to replicate the study, who provide their institutional affiliation, data management plan, and evidence of ethical approval where applicable; and 2) law enforcement personnel seeking to implement a similar prevention campaign, who provide their role and agency.
